questions.q: What does put-call parity state for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock?
questions.explain: Put-call parity is C - P = S - K*e^(-rT), where K*e^(-rT) is the present value of the strike price discounted at the risk-free rate.

questions.q: Put-call parity is derived by comparing which two portfolios?
options: A call alone versus a put alone
A call plus a bond that grows to K, versus a put plus one share of stock
A forward contract versus a futures contract
questions.explain: Portfolio A (call + bond worth K at expiration) and Portfolio B (put + stock) have identical payoffs of max(S, K) in every scenario, so their costs today must be equal — this gives parity.

questions.q: Why must two portfolios with identical payoffs in every future scenario have the same price today?
options: Because if their prices differed, you could sell the expensive one and buy the cheap one for a riskless, guaranteed profit — an arbitrage
Because both portfolios contain the same number of assets
This is only true for American options, not European options
questions.explain: This is the core no-arbitrage principle: a price difference between two positions with identical future payoffs would let someone lock in a riskless profit, which real markets compete away almost immediately.

questions.q: A stock trades at $40, strike is $40, r = 4% continuously compounded, T = 1 year, and the call is priced at $3.20. What does parity imply the fair put price should be (K*e^(-0.04) ≈ 38.43)?
If the market violates put-call parity, what is the practical consequence?
options: Nothing — parity is only a theoretical curiosity with no trading implications
The options exchange must halt trading
An arbitrageur can combine the mispriced options with the stock and a bond to lock in a riskless profit, and that trading activity pushes prices back toward parity
It proves the Black-Scholes model is wrong
questions.explain: A parity violation creates a real arbitrage opportunity. Exploiting it (buying the cheap side, selling the expensive side) is riskless and profitable, and that activity is exactly what keeps real-world prices close to parity.
